on-success.$description:
The tick on a checked checkbox (#1245). It has to flip with the theme:
--np-success is --np-sage, which is #6B7A5E in light and #A9BC98 in
dark, so white measures 4.59:1 on the first and 2.03:1 on the second --
under the 3:1 SC 1.4.11 floor for a non-text indicator. The pilot
components' hardcoded white tick had that fault and nothing could see
it, because check-contrast.mjs only scores the pairings it is told
about. It scores this one now.

on-info.$description:
Initials on a resource avatar (#1246/#1199). Single-valued, like the
hue tokens: --np-info is #108bb9 light and #3fb6e0 dark, and a dark ink
clears 4.5:1 on both (4.71 and 7.75) where white clears neither (3.88
and 2.36). Every avatar in the app painted white over
`var(--np-info-gradient)` -- a gradient, which check-contrast.mjs cannot
parse, so the one thing about an avatar that could be wrong was the one
thing nothing measured.

shadow-tint.$description:
--- Elevation (#1191). 105 distinct box-shadows today, most of them
one-off rgba() tuples a few hundredths apart. Four steps cover the
real cases: a hairline lift, a resting card, a floating menu, and a
modal over a dimmed page. The tint is a separate token so the ramp
darkens as a set in dark mode.

border-control.$description:
--- Control boundary (#1191). WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 wants 3:1 for the
visual boundary of a UI component. --np-border-strong is 1.33:1 against
the page, so an input outlined in it is invisible to a low-vision user.
It stays as-is for decorative separators, which the SC does not cover,
and this darker token is for anything with a boundary the user has to
find: inputs, selects, textareas, secondary buttons. 3.44:1 on paper.

link.$description:
--np-link and --np-link-hover were referenced by components.css but
defined nowhere, so links rendered the hardcoded #1976d2 fallback -- a
cool blue in a warm palette. Aliased onto the accent family instead
(#1192). .link-button also carries text-decoration: underline, so
colour is not the only thing marking a link (WCAG 1.4.1).

red.$description:
--- Identity palette (#1194, moved here from base.css).

The named hues predate the warm system and are not part of it: they are
the app's brand colours, used for RAG encodings, whiteboard note
categories and chart series, where the hue *is* the meaning. They live
here because every --np-* token does, not because they are surfaces.

Moving them changed nothing about where they resolve: a custom property
is resolved from the cascaded value on the element, not from where in the
file it was declared, so the var() references in base.css and the view
stylesheets -- all of which load earlier -- still pick them up.

link-highlight.$description:
#1271: the two-way hover link between a Gantt row and the markdown
line it came from. A state of its own, not a reuse of `:hover`
(--np-paper) or of `tr.selected` (--np-info-tint), because it has to
read as "this is the same task over there" from across two panes.

--np-yellow-subtle is the light value, but it cannot be used on its
own: it is declared only here and has no dark counterpart, so a row
painted with it in dark mode puts --np-ink (#FAF8F4) on #fff4d1 at
~1.03:1. The pair below is themed, and the ink is pinned rather than
inherited so the row's contrast does not depend on which theme's
--np-ink lands on it. Both pairings are scored by
scripts/check-contrast.mjs.

orange-ink.$description:
Ink for text sitting *on* a hue token. Single-valued like the hue it
pairs with -- the whole point of these is that the hue does not change
with the theme, so its ink cannot either. Added for the whiteboard
note's deliverable badge (#1248), whose rule had been carrying a raw
`#111` under a comment claiming `#161616`; scripts/check-contrast.mjs
now scores this pairing so the claim is measured rather than asserted.

accent-soft.$description:
--- Status ramp, overlay and shadow tints (#1194, moved here from
dark-mode.css, which is where the #1024 identity declared them).

## The palette decision, taken (#1194)

This block used to say the reconciliation was "deliberately left open".
It is now taken, and the app had half-taken it already: the RAG badge
rules at the foot of this file map rag-red to --np-danger-*, rag-amber
to --np-accent-* and rag-green to --np-sage-*. That is a complete
status ramp in the warm identity, written once for one component. The
decision is to name it and let everything else use it.

So: danger keeps its existing pair, success *is* sage, warning *is* the
marigold accent, and info takes the identity blue with a tint and ink
derived to sit in the same contrast band as the other three (light
4.8-6.3:1, dark 7.0-7.8:1 for ink-on-tint). The dark info tint is
#1C3A47, which is what --np-accent-soft already resolves to in dark --
the app had chosen it, it just had no name.

Every pairing here is gated by scripts/check-contrast.mjs.

One caveat worth carrying: --np-info on white is 3.88:1, which clears
AA for large text but *not* for body text. A filled info badge needs
large or bold type, or --np-info-ink on --np-info-tint instead.

avatar-bg.$description:
Resource avatars have their own pair rather than borrowing --np-info's.
A chip is a filled circle carrying two letters at ~9px; that is the
hardest text in the app to read, so it takes the strongest pairing the
app has rather than a status hue that also has to sit next to other
status hues. Near-black and white is 18.4:1 for the initials and 17.5:1
for the circle against the page -- both scored in
scripts/check-contrast.mjs.

Identity colour is not this chip's job. It never was: the avatars were
all one blue whoever they stood for, so the hue carried no information
and only had to be legible.

note-yellow-1.$description:
The whiteboard note palette (#1017, tokenised for #1250).
Two soft shades each of yellow, pink, green, blue and red. It is the
list wbPalette() offers in the note's colour menu and the list
wbDerivedPaletteColour() assigns from, and the values here are the
canonical ones -- whiteboard-notes.js's WB_NOTE_PASTEL_COLOURS is
checked against them by tests/test_note_ink.mjs.

They live here so scripts/check-contrast.mjs can score them, which it
could not while they were a JS array. Nothing had ever measured the
note's own de-emphasised text against its own fill, and three of those
pairings were below AA -- see --np-note-ink-muted below.

note-ink.$description:
A note's ink, and its two de-emphasis levels.
Every swatch above is light, so wbContrastTextColour() measures
--np-note-ink as the better of near-black/near-white on all ten; the
alpha values are the ones views/whiteboard.css mixes for
--wb-note-ink-muted and --wb-note-ink-faint, restated as literals so
the checker can composite them. b3 is 70% and 8c is 55%; the ink
ladder's comment in views/whiteboard.css explains why those two, and
tests/test_note_ink.mjs fails if the two files drift apart.

Not theme-flipped, and deliberately so: a note's ink is chosen against
the note's own fill, which is plan data and the same in both themes.

focus-ring-color.$description:
--- Focus ring (#1191). The app has 67 `outline: none` declarations and
five competing focus colours; buttons carry 242 :hover rules against 45
:focus ones.

The ring is two-layer on purpose. A single marigold ring is invisible
on a marigold button (1:1) and a single dark ring is invisible on a
dark page, so no one colour clears 3:1 everywhere. Painting an inner
halo in the page colour first means the ring always meets --np-paper,
whatever it is actually sitting on top of.

bg.$description: Bridge existing semantic consumers, including chart/table surface tokens.

editor-ink.$description:
The editor's text colour, previously a raw #d4d4d4 in views/gantt.css.
It is a token now so the band drawn behind it for #1271 has something
to be scored against.

editor-link-highlight.$description:
The #1271 band behind a linked markdown line. It cannot be
--np-link-highlight: that is light in the light theme, and the editor
is dark in *both* themes, so the light value would put #d4d4d4 text on
near-white. This is the dark-surface sibling of the same idea.
